 The Midterm Election Strengthened Democracy and Showed the Limits of Subversion Tactics
 In the November 2026 midterm elections, Americans across the nation produced massive pro-democracy results that both overcame election subversion attempts and bolstered chances for free and fair elections in 2028.

 Voters across the ideological spectrum delivered a stunning pro-democracy victory in the November midterm elections, with key stakeholders working together to thwart election subversion and voter suppression attempts by the Trump administration. Multiple factors contributed to this outcome, including state and local election officials who upheld the law, intense preparation by pro-democracy organizations and civil society, successful litigation, and, most importantly, the will of the American people.

 The overwhelming results, which saw Democratic candidates winning contests even in states that they had long lost, made the election too big to rig. These results will have continued benefits—namely, making it easier to defeat election sabotage efforts in 2028, even though the presidential-level election raises unique challenges that will require pro-democracy forces to remain organized and vigilant.
 The pro-democracy election results were unequivocal
 In a boon for democracy, the midterm elections were history-making in several respects, including huge voter interest and participation. A preliminary estimate concluded that at least 123 million people voted nationwide, comprising approximately 49 percent of eligible voters. This was the second-highest turnout in a midterm election since 1914. Turnout among minority and young voters was especially high. Given that the administration’s self-serving policies and election subversion attempts dominated the public debate for months, it is little surprise that voters ranked corruption and democracy as two of their top issues, aside from matters related to high costs.
 The election produced highly favorable results for Democrats, who flipped control of the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives. Although some jurisdictions are still waiting to count remaining votes, at the time of publication, Democrats had won 256 House seats compared with 170 for Republicans. And in the Senate, Democrats had won 55 seats compared with 44 for Republicans. Wins even occurred in traditionally conservative states such as Texas, Kansas, South Carolina, and Mississippi. Moreover, across key “battleground” states, Democrats won the top statewide offices , including governor, secretary of state, and attorney general. In the national House vote, Democrats currently lead by almost 14 percentage points , the largest midterm margin for either major political party since 1974 .
 State and local officials adeptly administered election contests. There were no widespread reports of equipment malfunctions or violence or threats at polling locations that significantly hampered Americans’ ability to vote. Perhaps most notably, despite the Trump administration’s multiple steps to try to subvert the election, which the Center for American Progress has documented in multiple articles , the election was free and fair—while reflecting the will of the people. Even in the face of well-founded concerns that the Trump administration may deploy the military or federal personnel , seize voting equipment, or declare a national emergency to unconstitutionally assert unilateral control over the election, these events did not occur.
 On election night, President Donald Trump accepted the results , but in recent days, he has begun to baselessly resurrect claims of widespread fraud and vote manipulation. It remains to be seen what actions the administration or its allies may take in the coming weeks and whether they may yet try to unlawfully interfere with vote counting and certification processes or baselessly prosecute state or local election officials. However, the threat of these types of illegal actions diminishes by the day, especially because the election system—and the many steps taken by pro-democracy stakeholders and the courts to fortify it against attack—proved resilient.
 Strong preparation helped defeat election subversion
 The administration’s attempts at election sabotage and voter suppression did not simply dissipate on their own. Instead, pro-democracy stakeholders spent months preparing to defend free and fair elections and then following through. These successful efforts, in turn, may have dissuaded the administration from further overreach. These pro-democracy efforts included:
 Pro-voter organizations partnered with a vast array of civil society stakeholders to preframe election subversion threats and educate everyday Americans about the laws that protect their vote. Subsequently, stakeholders took quick action when potential threats emerged. For example, after National Guard troops in Washington, D.C., were seen near a ballot drop box in the weeks before Election Day, public outcry coupled with official requests forced military commanders to issue a statement explicitly directing troops “not to monitor or secure polling locations” and to conduct their missions consistent with people’s constitutional rights.
 Pro-democracy organizations representing voters and other stakeholders expended vast resources to block unconstitutional or illegal efforts, as discussed in a prior CAP article . This included successfully litigating against the administration in dozens of cases , for example, where the administration attempted to force states to turn over their voter files, tried to compel California election officials to segregate ballots the administration deemed potentially fraudulent, and issued unconstitutional executive orders to unilaterally change election rules. Even the U.S. Supreme Court, in a much-watched case, blocked the administration’s relentless effort to neuter mail voting and weaponize the U.S. Postal Service against voters.
 Efforts to disenfranchise Black voters appear to have backfired, instead galvanizing Black organizing and turnout. This appears especially true in the South , according to compelling evidence . Moreover, the Supreme Court’s landmark April 2026 decision in Louisiana v. Callais , an anti-democracy case that undermines the Voting Rights Act and makes it much harder to stop racial gerrymandering, reportedly motivated additional Black voters to overcome the hurdles designed to deny them fair representation.
 Millions of Americans of all political stripes engaged in historic levels of peaceful protest in the months leading up to the election, including via “No Kings” rallies held in every state. These mobilizations, which educated people about threats to democracy and organized them to vote early , were a likely factor in increasing voter turnout.
 State and local officials—both Democratic and Republican—worked alongside community-based poll workers and volunteers amid unprecedented threats and legal actions from the federal government. Officials engaged in extensive pre-planning , strictly followed their legal duties to administer elections, and protected institutional safeguards. Members of Congress also took multiple steps to fight the administration’s subversion efforts, including by using their bully pulpits to shape public debate.
 These factors helped spur important victories across the nation, including in many deeply conservative states and districts, and ultimately led to the failure of the administration’s unprecedented mid-decade gerrymandering gambit in House districts. Just hours after the polls closed on Election Day, it became clear that the election was too big for the administration to rig, which a Trump adviser admitted the next day.

 Conclusion
 Despite substantial challenges, the 2026 midterm election marks a successful chapter in the ongoing quest to safeguard the will of the people to choose their leaders, a hallmark of a functioning democracy. Although it is unclear what subversion attempts, if any, the administration may try to take in the coming weeks before a new Congress is seated on January 3, 2027, such attempts will almost certainly continue to fail.
 Yet the 2028 presidential election lies ahead. Unique circumstances may present themselves, such as nefarious foreign interference. It is also possible that the administration will become more aggressive or creative in its attempts to manufacture election results, including via certification processes tied to the Electoral College—processes that Trump and his allies tried to exploit in 2020 . The damage wrought by election denialism still endures.
 However, one major bulwark against 2028 election sabotage will be the slate of Democratic governors, secretaries of state, and other executive positions that voters just chose to lead the battleground states, where the stakes of democracy are often under the most pressure. These state-level officials, allied with pro-democracy Republican officials in other states, voting rights organizations and other civil society organizations, courts, and the American people, will fight to protect a free and fair election in 2028.
 The positions of American Progress, and our policy experts, are independent, and the findings and conclusions presented are those of American Progress alone. American Progress would like to acknowledge the many generous supporters who make our work possible.
